interactions.label: Why can fatty acids not contribute carbon to gluconeogenesis?

params.question: Why can fatty acids not contribute carbon to gluconeogenesis?

answers.text: Fatty acids are converted to pyruvate, which inhibits gluconeogenic enzymes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fatty acids undergo β-oxidation to produce acetyl-CoA, not pyruvate. There is no pathway converting fatty acids to pyruvate in humans.

answers.text: The conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA carbons from β-oxidation cannot form glucose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pyruvate dehydrogenase catalyses an irreversible decarboxylation. Once carbons enter the acetyl-CoA pool via β-oxidation, they can only be oxidised in the TCA cycle or diverted to ketogenesis — never reconverted to glucose.

answers.text: Fatty acids lack sufficient carbon atoms to assemble a glucose molecule

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fatty acids have plenty of carbons (e.g., palmitate has 16). The limitation is biochemical irreversibility at the pyruvate dehydrogenase step, not carbon number.

answers.text: Hepatocytes do not take up fatty acids during the fasting state

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hepatocytes actively take up and oxidise fatty acids during fasting — this is precisely how they generate ketone bodies and energy for gluconeogenesis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember that pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (via pyruvate dehydrogenase) is an irreversible step. Since β-oxidation of fatty acids produces acetyl-CoA, those carbons are permanently committed to oxidation and cannot be used to synthesise glucose.

The irreversibility of the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is a cornerstone of metabolic integration. It explains why the body must break down muscle protein for gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting, since fat stores alone cannot supply glucose.

interactions.label: A patient with type 1 diabetes presents with Kussmaul breathing and fruity-smell

params.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes presents with Kussmaul breathing and fruity-smelling breath. Which metabolic process is primarily responsible for this presentation?

answers.text: Excessive hepatic glycogenolysis causing severe hyperglycaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Glycogenolysis contributes to hyperglycaemia but does not explain the acidosis. Kussmaul breathing and fruity breath indicate ketoacidosis, not simple hyperglycaemia.

answers.text: Accelerated gluconeogenesis from branched-chain amino acids

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gluconeogenesis does increase in DKA, but the acidosis and fruity breath are caused by accumulation of ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone), not by amino acid metabolism.

answers.text: Unchecked lipolysis and ketogenesis due to absolute insulin deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Without insulin, glucagon drives unopposed lipolysis. The resulting flood of fatty acids overwhelms hepatic β-oxidation, producing excess acetyl-CoA that is diverted to ketone bodies. Blood pH falls below 7.1, triggering compensatory Kussmaul breathing, and acetone gives the characteristic fruity odour.

answers.text: Refeeding-induced electrolyte shifts causing metabolic acidosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Refeeding syndrome causes hypophosphataemia and hypokalaemia when nutrition is restored to a starved patient — the opposite clinical scenario. It does not produce ketoacidosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: In type 1 diabetes without insulin, the body cannot sense its high blood glucose. Glucagon acts unopposed, driving lipolysis and ketogenesis. The resulting accumulation of ketone bodies causes the metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul breathing, and fruity breath characteristic of DKA.

DKA demonstrates what happens when metabolic integration fails. Absent insulin mimics starvation signals despite abundant blood glucose, driving maximal fat breakdown and unchecked ketone body production. Treatment requires insulin, fluids, and potassium.

interactions.label: Which property of the inner mitochondrial membrane is essential for generating t

params.question: Which property of the inner mitochondrial membrane is essential for generating the proton-motive force used in ATP synthesis?

answers.text: It contains porins that allow free passage of small molecules

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Porins are present in the outer mitochondrial membrane, making it permeable. The inner membrane must be impermeable for the proton gradient to accumulate.

answers.text: It is highly impermeable to protons, preventing their free diffusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The inner mitochondrial membrane is highly impermeable — even protons cannot cross it freely. This allows ETC complexes to pump protons into the intermembrane space and maintain the electrochemical gradient that drives ATP synthase.

answers.text: It is folded into cristae that house the TCA cycle enzymes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cristae do increase surface area for ETC complexes and ATP synthase, but TCA cycle enzymes reside in the matrix, not in the membrane. The critical property for the proton gradient is impermeability.

answers.text: It is permeable to NADH, allowing direct electron delivery from the cytoplasm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The inner membrane is impermeable to NADH. Cytoplasmic NADH must use shuttle systems (e.g., the malate-aspartate shuttle) to transfer its reducing equivalents into the mitochondrial matrix.

overallFeedback.feedback: The inner mitochondrial membrane must be impermeable to protons so that ETC complexes I, III, and IV can pump protons into the intermembrane space and build the electrochemical gradient (~200 mV) that powers ATP synthesis.

The impermeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane is the physical basis of chemiosmotic coupling. Without it, protons pumped by the ETC would diffuse back freely, and no gradient could be maintained to drive ATP synthase.

interactions.label: Complex II of the electron transport chain pumps protons across the inner mitoch

params.question: Complex II of the electron transport chain pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Complex II is unique among ETC complexes because it does not pump protons. It transfers electrons from succinate → FAD → iron-sulphur clusters → coenzyme Q, but the energy change is too small for transmembrane proton translocation. This is precisely why FADH₂ yields fewer ATP molecules than NADH.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) transfers electrons from succinate via FAD and iron-sulphur clusters to coenzyme Q, but the free energy released is insufficient to drive proton pumping. This is why electrons entering at Complex II yield only ~1.5 ATP, compared to ~2.5 for NADH entering at Complex I.

interactions.label: A family is brought to the emergency department after using a charcoal heater in

params.question: A family is brought to the emergency department after using a charcoal heater in a closed room during winter. Which step in the electron transport chain is directly blocked by the causative agent?

answers.text: Electron transfer from NADH to coenzyme Q at Complex I

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complex I is inhibited by rotenone, barbiturates, and MPTP — not by carbon monoxide. The clinical scenario describes CO poisoning from incomplete combustion of charcoal.

answers.text: Oxidation of succinate to fumarate at Complex II

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complex II is not a target of carbon monoxide. Mutations in its subunits are linked to hereditary paragangliomas, but CO does not affect this complex.

answers.text: The Q cycle at Complex III

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complex III is inhibited by antimycin A, which blocks the Qi site. Carbon monoxide does not target Complex III.

answers.text: Reduction of oxygen to water at Complex IV

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Carbon monoxide binds to haem a₃ in Complex IV — the same site where oxygen normally binds and is reduced to water. This halts the entire electron transport chain. CO also binds haemoglobin with 200 times the affinity of oxygen, worsening tissue hypoxia. Treatment includes high-flow oxygen.

overallFeedback.feedback: Carbon monoxide from incomplete charcoal combustion blocks Complex IV by binding to haem a₃, preventing oxygen from reaching the active site. Cyanide and hydrogen sulphide act by the same mechanism. All three poisons halt the final step of electron transport.

Charcoal heater poisoning in closed rooms is tragically common in Indian winters. Carbon monoxide blocks Complex IV at the haem a₃–CuB binuclear centre, the same site targeted by cyanide and hydrogen sulphide.

interactions.label: According to Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, what directly drives ATP synthe

params.question: According to Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, what directly drives ATP synthesis in mitochondria?

answers.text: A high-energy phosphorylated chemical intermediate linking the ETC to ATP synthase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This was the prevailing theory before Mitchell's work — that a high-energy intermediate directly coupled electron transport to phosphorylation. Mitchell disproved this, showing that the coupling is entirely indirect and mediated by the proton gradient.

answers.text: Direct transfer of electrons from cytochrome c to the catalytic site of ATP synthase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Electrons from cytochrome c are delivered to Complex IV for oxygen reduction, not to ATP synthase. ATP synthase is driven by proton flow, not electron flow.

answers.text: The electrochemical proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Mitchell's key insight was that coupling is indirect. ETC complexes pump protons to create an electrochemical gradient (~200 mV) across the inner membrane. Protons flow back through ATP synthase, and that flow — not any chemical intermediate — drives ATP synthesis.

answers.text: Substrate-level phosphorylation catalysed by succinyl-CoA synthetase in the matrix

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Substrate-level phosphorylation occurs at specific steps in glycolysis and the TCA cycle. It is independent of the proton gradient and accounts for only a small fraction of total cellular ATP production.

overallFeedback.feedback: The chemiosmotic hypothesis states that ETC complexes I, III, and IV pump protons out of the matrix, creating an electrochemical gradient (the proton-motive force). Protons flow back through ATP synthase, and that flow — not any chemical intermediate — is what drives ATP synthesis.

Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis — ridiculed for two decades before earning the 1978 Nobel Prize — established that biological energy conversion uses an electrochemical gradient rather than a chemical intermediate. This principle applies universally across mitochondria, chloroplasts, and bacterial membranes.

interactions.label: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) was used as a weight-loss drug in the 1930s but caused f

params.question: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) was used as a weight-loss drug in the 1930s but caused fatal hyperthermia. What is its mechanism of action?

answers.text: It blocks Complex IV, preventing oxygen consumption and causing energy failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complex IV inhibitors (cyanide, CO) stop electron transport entirely. DNP does the opposite — the ETC runs at maximum speed because the proton gradient is continuously dissipated and the chain works harder to rebuild it.

answers.text: It inhibits the proton channel of ATP synthase, halting ATP production

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes oligomycin, which blocks the F₀ proton channel. Oligomycin causes the proton gradient to build up excessively, slowing oxygen consumption — the opposite of what DNP does.

answers.text: It carries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. DNP is a lipid-soluble weak acid that shuttles protons across the inner membrane without passing through ATP synthase. The ETC runs at full speed, consuming oxygen and oxidising fuels, but no ATP is made — all energy is released as heat, causing fatal hyperthermia. UCP-1 (thermogenin) in brown adipose tissue uses this same principle physiologically for non-shivering thermogenesis in newborns.

answers.text: It inhibits Complex I, forcing cells to rely entirely on anaerobic glycolysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complex I inhibitors (rotenone, barbiturates) block electron flow. DNP does not block any complex — it dissipates the proton gradient itself, allowing electron flow to accelerate rather than stop.

overallFeedback.feedback: DNP is an uncoupler — a lipid-soluble weak acid that ferries protons across the inner membrane, short-circuiting ATP synthase. The ETC accelerates and oxygen consumption rises, but all energy is released as heat rather than captured as ATP, causing dangerous hyperthermia.

DNP illustrates the critical distinction between ETC inhibitors and uncouplers. Inhibitors block electron flow and stop oxygen consumption; uncouplers dissipate the proton gradient, accelerating oxygen consumption but wasting energy as heat. The body uses this same principle via UCP-1 in brown fat for newborn thermogenesis.
